paras.text: Plans, Estimating Math, Trade Boundaries and Permits, Audio Lecture

This is the second biggest block of the trade exam. Plans, specifications, and estimating are fourteen of the one hundred ten trade questions. On top of that, this chapter covers trade boundaries, meaning what you may not touch without a plumbing, electrical, or mechanical license, and the permit and inspection process, which shows up on the business and law side too.

Here is the good news about this chapter. Almost every question in the estimating half is a formula with numbers plugged into it. There is no interpretation and no judgment. If you can run the formula, you get the point, and I am going to run each one out loud with you rather than just naming it.

Everything keys to the twenty fifteen Michigan Residential Code. The twenty twenty one update was stayed by a court in July of twenty twenty five and never took effect, so if an answer choice smells like the newer national code, be suspicious of it.
Idea one. Reading the drawings.
Floor plans and elevations are drawn at one quarter inch equals one foot. That is the single most tested scale fact on this exam.
And it gives you a shortcut worth knowing. On a quarter scale plan, multiply the plan inches by four and you get real feet. Six inches on the paper is twenty four feet of real wall.

Site plans are different. They use an engineer's scale, usually one inch equals twenty feet or one inch equals thirty feet. And details, like a stair connection or a flashing condition, get drawn much bigger, anywhere from three quarters of an inch up to three inches equals one foot.
Now the drawing types, and the way to keep them straight is to ask what each one shows you.
An elevation is a flat picture of the outside face of the house. Finishes, window and door openings, the grade line, the roof slope.
A section is a vertical cut through the building, and it is where you find what is inside the wall or floor. Sheathing, studs, insulation, floor to floor heights.
So if the question asks where you would find the layers of a wall assembly, the answer is the wall section. Elevation shows the face, section shows the guts.
A detail is a blow up of one small condition, referenced by a bubble. If you see the number three over the letters A five in a circle, that means detail three, drawn on sheet A five.
And sheet prefixes matter. A is architectural. S is structural. M is mechanical. E is electrical. P is plumbing. C is civil.
Idea two. What wins when the documents disagree.
Two rules, and the exam likes both.
First, a written dimension always beats a scaled measurement. Never scale a drawing when the number is printed on it. Paper stretches, prints shrink, and the writer meant the number.

Second, when the drawings and the written specifications disagree, the specifications generally govern. But note what the best exam answer usually is, notify the architect and get clarification before you proceed. On a test that offers you both, the professional answer wins.
And remember the division of labor between the two documents. Specs control quality. Drawings control quantity and location.

Schedules are the tables keyed to marks on the plan. A window called out as three zero five zero is three feet zero inches wide by five feet zero inches high. Width first, then height. A door marked two eight six eight is two feet eight inches by six feet eight inches.

For specifications, know the classic sixteen division C S I MasterFormat. The ones that get tested are division three concrete, division four masonry, division six wood and plastics, division seven thermal and moisture protection, division eight doors and windows, division nine finishes, division fifteen mechanical, and division sixteen electrical.
Idea three. The estimating formulas, run out loud.
Board feet first. Board feet equals thickness in inches, times width in inches, times length in feet, divided by twelve.
Run it. A two by six that is ten feet long. Two times six is twelve, times ten is one hundred twenty, divided by twelve is ten board feet.

And lumber is priced per thousand board feet, so the pricing question has one extra step. Eight hundred board feet at six hundred dollars per thousand is point eight times six hundred, which is four hundred eighty dollars.
Concrete. Twenty seven cubic feet make one cubic yard. Length times width times thickness, all in feet, divided by twenty seven. Convert inches to feet first, so four inches is a third of a foot.

Run it. A twenty by thirty slab at four inches. Twenty times thirty is six hundred, times one third is two hundred cubic feet. Divided by twenty seven is seven point four yards. Add five to ten percent waste and round up, so you order eight.
And that is the general rule on any ordering question. Round up. Never order short. The exam is not testing whether you can shave a yard.

Masonry has two magic numbers. Standard modular brick runs six point seven five bricks per square foot of wall. Standard eight by eight by sixteen block runs one point one two five blocks per square foot.
Run both. A thousand square foot wall with a hundred square feet of openings is nine hundred net. Nine hundred times six point seven five is six thousand seventy five bricks.
And a forty foot wall, eight feet tall, is three hundred twenty square feet. Times one point one two five is three hundred sixty blocks.

Roofing is counted in squares, and a square is one hundred square feet. A twenty four hundred square foot roof is twenty four squares. Standard three tab shingles run three bundles per square, so that is seventy two bundles, plus roughly ten percent waste.
Drywall and sheathing come in four by eight sheets, which is thirty two square feet each. Total your wall and ceiling area, divide by thirty two, round up, add waste.

Framing counts. Studs at sixteen inches on center, take the wall length in feet, multiply by three quarters, add one, then add extras for corners and openings. The fast field rule is one stud per lineal foot of wall, which builds in the extras.
Joists work the same way. A twenty four foot run at sixteen on center is twenty four times point seven five, which is eighteen, plus one, so nineteen joists.
Plates are three times the wall length, because you have one bottom plate and a double top.
Question. How many board feet in a two by eight that is twelve feet long, and how many joists at sixteen on center across a thirty two foot run.
Two times eight times twelve is one hundred ninety two, divided by twelve is sixteen board feet. And thirty two times point seven five is twenty four, plus one, so twenty five joists.
Idea four. Excavation, where the trap is in the direction of the math.
Soil swells when you dig it and shrinks when you compact it, so the same dirt has three different volumes depending on where it is.
Bank yards are in the ground. Loose yards are in the truck. Compacted yards are in the fill.
Common earth swells about twenty five percent. So one hundred bank yards becomes one hundred twenty five loose yards to haul.

Now the trap, and it is the same shape as the markup and margin trap from the business chapter. If you need one hundred compacted yards and shrinkage is ten percent, you divide by point nine, which gives about one hundred eleven bank yards.
You divide by one minus the shrinkage. You do not just add ten percent. Adding ten percent gives one hundred ten, and it is wrong for the same reason multiplying was wrong on margin.
Idea five. Grade and slope.
Percent grade is rise over run, times one hundred. Two feet of fall in one hundred feet is two percent.
Two conversions worth memorizing. A quarter inch per foot is about two percent. An eighth inch per foot is about one percent, and that is your garage floor slope.

And the code number you already know from the foundation chapter, the ground must fall six inches in the first ten feet away from the foundation, which is five percent, or two percent minimum on pavement.
Idea six. The stair problem, which is the money question.
This is the calculation most likely to appear, and Michigan differs from the national code, so run it my way.
Michigan allows a maximum riser of eight and one quarter inches and a minimum tread of nine inches. The national I R C numbers, seven and three quarters and ten inches, are the trap answers.
Here is the method, four steps.
Step one. Total rise divided by the maximum riser, then round up. That gives your riser count.
Step two. Total rise divided by that riser count gives the actual riser height.
Step three. Treads are always one fewer than risers.
Step four. Treads times the minimum tread depth gives the minimum total run.
Now run it. Floor to floor rise is one hundred eight inches. Divide by eight point two five and you get thirteen point zero nine. Round up to fourteen risers.
The actual riser is one hundred eight divided by fourteen, which is about seven point seven inches. Treads are thirteen, and at nine inches each the minimum total run is one hundred seventeen inches.

Now understand why you round up, because that is the real question hiding inside the arithmetic. If you rounded down to thirteen risers, each one would be one hundred eight divided by thirteen, which is eight point three one inches. That is over the eight and a quarter maximum, so it is illegal. Rounding up is what keeps you under the limit.
And one more stair number you already have, risers and treads cannot vary more than three eighths of an inch within a flight.
Question. Total rise is ninety nine inches. How many risers, and how tall is each one.

Ninety nine divided by eight point two five is exactly twelve, so twelve risers at eight and a quarter inches, right at the maximum. Eleven treads. If the number had come out at twelve point one, you would round up to thirteen.
Idea seven. Trade boundaries, and what your license does not let you do.

Your residential builder license lets you build the house and lets you coordinate the job. It never lets you do plumbing, electrical, or mechanical work. Each of those trades has its own license, its own permit, and its own inspections.
All three are now licensed under one law, the Skilled Trades Regulation Act, Act four zero seven of twenty sixteen, which replaced the old separate trade acts.
Plumbing runs apprentice, then journeyman at six thousand hours over three years, then master with four thousand more hours over two years.
Electrical runs journeyman at eight thousand hours over four years, then master at twelve thousand hours over six years, including two years as a journeyman.

And in both trades, the contracting business itself needs a separate contractor license, and it must employ a master. Hear that distinction, because it is tested. A master license alone does not make you a contractor.

Now mechanical, which is the odd one and a favorite trap. Under the same act, Michigan licenses the mechanical contractor as a business entity only. There is no individual journeyman or master mechanical license in Michigan. The company designates a qualifying officer and carries classification endorsements for the kinds of work it does.
So if an answer choice mentions a Michigan master mechanical license, it is wrong. There is no such thing.
And anyone handling refrigerant also needs federal E P A section six zero eight certification.

The homeowner exemption. A homeowner may do their own trade work on their own primary residence, under their own permit. Rentals are excluded. And a contractor may never work under a homeowner's permit. That is illegal, and it is a common real world scheme that the exam expects you to reject.
Your job as the builder is to hire licensed subs, verify their licenses on the LARA website before they start, make sure they pull their own permits, and sequence their inspections.
Question. Does Michigan issue a master mechanical license to an individual, and can your plumbing sub work under the homeowner's permit.
No to both. Mechanical is licensed to the business entity only, with a qualifying officer. And a contractor may never work under a homeowner's permit.
Idea eight. Permits, and the exemption list.
The governing law is Act two thirty of nineteen seventy two, the Stille DeRossett Hale Single State Construction Code Act.
No regulated work starts before a permit is issued. Ever.
But some work is exempt, under section R one zero five point two, and this list is pure memorization, so here it is.

A one story detached accessory structure, like a shed, up to two hundred square feet. A fence up to seven feet high. A retaining wall up to four feet, measured from the bottom of the footing, that holds back no surcharge. Sidewalks and driveways not more than thirty inches above grade. Painting, papering, tiling, carpeting, cabinets, and countertops. Above ground prefab pools less than twenty four inches deep. Window awnings projecting fifty four inches or less. And decks of two hundred square feet or less that sit no more than thirty inches above grade and do not serve the exit door.
Watch the shed trap. Two hundred square feet is the current number. One twenty is the old code, and it is sitting in a lot of study material.
Now the timelines.
The building department has ten business days to issue or deny a permit, and fifteen for an unusually complicated building or structure.
An issued permit dies if work does not start within one hundred eighty days, or if work stops for one hundred eighty days.
The certificate of occupancy must be issued within five business days of written application, once every permit is finaled, every inspection passed, and every fee paid.
And sealed architect plans are not required for one and two family dwellings under three thousand five hundred square feet.
Idea nine. Inspections, and the one rule that is never negotiable.

The sequence runs footing and foundation before the pour. Waterproofing before backfill. Rough framing. Then rough electrical, plumbing, and mechanical before anything is covered. Then insulation. Then drywall. Then the four finals. Then the certificate of occupancy.
Notice the pattern, every inspection happens at the last moment the work is still visible. That is the logic of the whole sequence, and it gives you the iron rule.
Never cover uninspected work.
If you do, the inspector can issue a stop work order and make you tear it open. And after a stop work order, the only work allowed is what makes the site safe.

Penalties. A knowing violation is a misdemeanor, up to five hundred dollars and up to ninety days. Each knowing violation is a separate offense. And each day counts as a separate offense specifically when you keep working through a stop construction order.
Unlicensed residential work draws a separate civil fine of one hundred to five hundred dollars.
Rapid fire recap. Say these with me.

Quarter inch equals one foot for floor plans. One inch equals twenty or thirty feet for site plans. Window three zero five zero is three feet by five feet, width first. Board feet is thickness times width times length over twelve. Twenty seven cubic feet in a yard, five to ten percent concrete waste. Six point seven five bricks per square foot. One point one two five blocks per square foot. A roofing square is one hundred square feet, three bundles per square. A four by eight sheet is thirty two square feet. Studs at sixteen on center, length times point seven five plus one. Common earth swells twenty five percent, and you divide by one minus the shrinkage. Grade is rise over run times one hundred, and six inches in ten feet away from the house. Michigan riser eight and a quarter maximum, tread nine minimum, variance three eighths, treads equal risers minus one, and always round the riser count up. Plumber hours, six thousand journeyman, four thousand more for master. Electrician hours, eight thousand journeyman, twelve thousand master. No individual mechanical license, entity only, with a qualifying officer. Permit exemptions, shed two hundred square feet, fence seven feet, retaining wall four feet, deck two hundred square feet under thirty inches, awning fifty four inches. Permit in ten business days, dead after one hundred eighty idle days, certificate of occupancy in five business days, sealed plans only at thirty five hundred square feet and up. And never cover uninspected work.

Fourteen questions here, and the two that will decide them are the stair calculation, because it has four steps and a rounding rule, and the excavation shrinkage, because it is the same divide, do not multiply trap you met in the business chapter. Drill those two until they are boring.
